extracted.intended_audience: PR/marketing professionals, startup founders, comms teams writing press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Crafting press releases designed to be picked up widely and go viral: concise layered structure, a strong hook, a tweetable stat/quote, and distribution timing/embargo tactics to maximize pickup and follow-on coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional reaction
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A release should provoke an emotional response that motivates sharing. Counter-intuitive findings, personal stakes, David-vs-Goliath framing, concrete villains, and money figures are examples of emotional triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication reporter sharing (embargo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gets shared by reporters BEFORE it's published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brief 2-3 trusted reporters under embargo first so they have the story and may share it immediately when published. Early reporter buy-in is a key signal of viral potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tweetable moment / quotable stat or quote
rubrics_metrics.description: Has a 'tweetable' moment — one stat or quote that fits in 280 characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide one concise stat or quote that reporters and social users can lift and share. Place a clear quote near the end (see 'Quotable placement') and prefer concrete numbers over hedged language. The tweetable moment should be immediately clear and pithy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hashtag-worthy phrase
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a short, catchy phrase that can be turned into a hashtag to help aggregation and social visibility. Avoid bloated corporate phrasing that can't be shortened into a hashtag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spawns follow-on coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Spawns thinkpieces and reaction articles for days afterward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for themes or tensions (e.g., generational framing, clear villains, societal stakes) that invite commentary and prolonged discussion, not just a single pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hook within first 50 words
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hook (first 50 words) should include a surprising stat + clear stakes + name a recognizable entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer 1 — The Hook (first 50 words). Don't bury the lede; put the surprising/statistical insight, why it matters, and a recognizable name/entity up front so editors immediately grasp newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance in next ~150 words
rubrics_metrics.description: The Substance (next 150 words) should provide supporting detail: methodology if data; timeline if news; before/after if change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer 2 — The Substance (next 150 words). Be concise and concrete about how the finding was produced or what happened; avoid jargon and hedging. This section should satisfy basic reporter questions (how, when, who).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotable placement (final 100 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: One quote in the final ~100 words that a reporter could lift verbatim into the headline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer 3 — The Quotable (final 100 words). Provide a pithy, headline-ready quote attributed to a credible source. This is the quote reporters are most likely to use directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: David vs. Goliath framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the story as David vs. Goliath where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classic narrative creates clear stakes and an emotional ally or antagonist, making the story more compelling and shareable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter-intuitive finding
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprising or counter-expectation results drive curiosity and sharing. Ensure the surprise is supported by clear evidence in the Substance section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete villain
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming a specific target or source of the problem (rather than vague 'challenges') sharpens the narrative and fuels reaction pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal stakes for an identifiable group
rubrics_metrics.description: Show personal stakes for an identifiable group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear who is affected (e.g., parents, Gen Z workers) so readers have an emotional entry point and a reason to share with peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money figures / numerical anchor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use money figures (especially round numbers) or another concrete numerical anchor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete numbers (round figures preferred) make headlines and tweets. Avoid the anti-pattern of 'no real number in the headline'—put a real number front-and-center where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generational framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use generational framing when relevant (e.g., 'Gen Z is...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing findings around a generation or cohort creates ready-made audiences and narratives for commentary and sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing / day of release
rubrics_metrics.description: Schedule release for optimal pickup: time release for Tuesday-Thursday, 6-9am ET.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid Friday afternoon, before holidays, and major news days when your release will be overlooked. Timing influences both reporter availability and audience attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spokesperson availability at launch
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a spokesperson on standby for the first hour after release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate availability for comment increases chances reporters will use your quotes and publish quickly; arrange phone/email access for rapid follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid burying the lede
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the main news/insight appears in the first 50 words (see Hook). Burying key information reduces immediate editor interest and kills virality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote credibility / attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes must be attributed to someone important/credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid quotes attributed to no one important—credible spokespeople increase pickup and headline-worthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid corporate hedging language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid too much corporate hedging language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hedged, cautious corporate-speak undermines shareability and makes headlines bland. Use clear, assertive phrasing for the hook and quote.
